meta.title: Who really said "History Does Not Repeat Itself. The Historians Repeat One Another"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Oscar Wilde. Max Beerbohm printed this wording in 1896 — and flagged it as already current. Quote Investigator traces the idea back to 1868.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'History Does Not Repeat Itself. The Historians Repeat One Another'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Oscar Wilde. Max Beerbohm printed it in 1896 but said it was already a saying. The Wilde credit starts as a 1912 coin toss and hardens in one uncited 1988 footnote.

answer.label: Not Oscar Wilde — printed by Max Beerbohm, 1896
answer.sourceLine: The exact wording opens Beerbohm’s essay “1880” in The Works of Max Beerbohm (1896) — but he printed it as a quotation, prefaced “it has been said,” explicitly disclaiming coinage. Quote Investigator finds no precise origin for the saying and no trace of it in Oscar Wilde’s work; the Wilde credit surfaces only in 1912, as one half of a guess.

source.excerpt: “History,” it has been said, “does not repeat itself. The historians repeat one another.” Now, there are still some periods with which no historian has grappled, and, strangely enough, the period that most greatly fascinates me is one of them. The labour I set myself is therefore rather Herculean.
trail: 1868 — The oldest relative on record is anonymous. An item from the Louisville Journal, reprinted on 30 June 1868 in the Atlanta Constitution and The Charleston Daily News, ran: “History will, of course, go on repeating itself, and the historians repeating each other.” This is the earliest evidence located by Quote Investigator ↗.

1896 — Max Beerbohm opens his essay “1880” with the polished antithetical form, in quotation marks and credited to no one: “‘History,’ it has been said, ‘does not repeat itself. The historians repeat one another.’” Verifiable in the full text at Project Gutenberg ↗.

1912 — Robert Lynd, reviewing a book in The Nation, becomes the first writer known to link the line to Wilde — and does so by hedging: “said either Wilde or Mr. Max Beerbohm.” Quote Investigator dates and transcribes the passage ↗.

1988 — Richard Ellmann’s Oscar Wilde puts a version in a footnote as Wilde’s own, with no citation; researchers have since been unable to find it in Wilde’s work ↗. That footnote is the ancestor of every “Oscar Wilde” graphic online today.
source.excerptNote: Beerbohm dated the essay “London, 1894” at its foot, and an earlier version had run in The Yellow Book, vol. 4 (January 1895). This opening sentence does not appear in Yellow Nineties 2.0’s transcription of that periodical text ↗, which begins differently — so the 1896 book, whose text is readable in full at Project Gutenberg ↗, is the printing to cite.

source.rightsNote: The wording quoted here is taken from The Works of Max Beerbohm, first published in 1896 — comfortably before 1931, so the text is in the public domain in the United States, and Project Gutenberg distributes it freely ↗. The saying itself is older still and anonymous; Richard Ellmann’s 1988 phrasing of it, by contrast, sits inside an in-copyright biography and is not reproduced here beyond the short quotation needed to identify the error.

author.name: Max Beerbohm
author.heading: Max Beerbohm — the wit who said it wasn't his
author.bio: Max Beerbohm was the great miniaturist of English letters — a caricaturist and essayist who published his collected works at twenty-four and titled the closing essay “Diminuendo.” He belonged to the 1890s Yellow Book circle that also orbited Oscar Wilde, which is precisely why the two men’s epigrams have been swapped for a century. On this one Beerbohm was scrupulous: he set the sentence in quotation marks and credited it to nobody, because by 1896 it was already common property.

copyAttribution: "History does not repeat itself. The historians repeat one another." — not Oscar Wilde. Max Beerbohm printed this exact wording in his essay "1880," in The Works of Max Beerbohm (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1896), 41 — but flagged it as already current with the words "it has been said." Quote Investigator finds no precise origin, and none of it in Wilde's work; the earliest attachment to Wilde known to QI is a 1912 review that guessed "either Wilde or Mr. Max Beerbohm."

misattribution.heading: How Wilde got the credit
misattribution.intro: Nobody in the saying’s own era claimed to know who wrote it. The Wilde attribution arrives late, arrives hedged, and hardens only in the twentieth century’s standard Wilde biography.

items.scope: The wording that circulates as Wilde’s
items.why: Richard Ellmann’s 1988 biography Oscar Wilde attributes “History never repeats itself. The historians repeat each other. There is a wide difference” to Wilde in a footnote — but, as Quote Investigator records ↗, Ellmann gave no supporting citation and other researchers have been unable to find the expression anywhere in Wilde’s work.

items.scope: The first time Wilde’s name was attached at all
items.why: In a book review in the London periodical The Nation (29 June 1912), the Irish essayist Robert Lynd wrote: “‘History does not repeat itself,’ said either Wilde or Mr. Max Beerbohm; ‘historians repeat each other.’” Quote Investigator calls this the earliest attachment to Wilde known to it ↗ — and it is a coin toss, not a citation.

items.scope: The other names it has been pinned on
items.why: Guedalla’s 1914 New Statesman piece offered “Quintilian or Mr. Max Beerbohm”; a Navy Records Society editor the same year called it “the mot ascribed to Mr. Max Beerbohm”; and Rupert Brooke, in a letter of 4 June 1906, believed he had made up his own version. Guedalla was passing the line on, not claiming it — like Beerbohm, he disclaimed originating it. All three claims are laid out by Quote Investigator ↗, and all of them postdate the anonymous 1868 forerunner.

items.scope: Where the Wilde version lives now
items.why: Ellmann’s footnote wording is what the aggregators reprint. AllGreatQuotes ↗, for instance, runs “History never repeats itself. The historians repeat each other. There is a wide difference. – Oscar Wilde” with no work, date or source of any kind attached.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence you are looking for is real, and it is in print in 1896 — but it belongs to no one. Beerbohm set it in quotation marks and credited it to nobody, and Quote Investigator’s conclusion is that the saying is proverbial, with no precise ascription currently known ↗.

context.heading: Why this one keeps landing on Wilde
lead: The epigram is built the way a Wilde epigram is built — a flat statement, then a reversal that makes the first half the joke. It is short, it is cynical about experts, and it flatters the reader for getting it. That shape is enough. Lines with that shape drift toward the two or three names the public keeps on file for “Victorian wit,” and Wilde is the first drawer anyone opens.

The drift is unusually well documented here. In 1912 the Irish essayist Robert Lynd printed the line and could only say it was “either Wilde or Mr. Max Beerbohm.” Two years later Philip Guedalla hedged between Quintilian and Beerbohm; the same year a Navy Records Society editor simply handed it to Beerbohm. Nobody in the saying’s own era claimed to know. Then in 1988 Richard Ellmann, in the standard Wilde biography, put a version in a footnote with no citation attached — and the guess hardened into a fact.
detailsBody: The oldest relative Quote Investigator has located is anonymous: an 1868 item from the Louisville Journal, reprinted in Atlanta and Charleston, musing that “History will, of course, go on repeating itself, and the historians repeating each other.” The polished antithetical form — history does not repeat, the historians do — appears in Beerbohm in 1896.

Between those poles the saying was clearly floating free. The poet Rupert Brooke thought he had coined a version of it in a letter of 4 June 1906. The historian Emil Reich played with both halves in Nights with the Gods (1908). The New York Times called it an “axiom” in 1923 and attributed it to nobody at all. A proverb, in other words, doing what proverbs do.
context.pull: Beerbohm put the sentence in quotation marks. Everyone who has quoted him since has taken the quotation marks off.

schema.alternateName: History never repeats itself. The historians repeat each other.
schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Oscar Wilde. Max Beerbohm printed this wording in 1896, but quoted it as an existing saying, prefaced “it has been said”; Quote Investigator finds both forms proverbial, with no precise ascription currently known. The 1896 printing is the earliest one carrying this exact wording, not the origin.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes both forms of the saying are proverbial with no precise ascription known; earliest evidence is an anonymous 1868 Louisville Journal item reprinted 30 June 1868 in Atlanta and Charleston reading 'History will, of course, go on repeating itself, and the historians repeating each other.'

Quote Investigator documents Beerbohm's 1896 essay '1880' using the wording with 'it has been said' (disclaiming coinage); Rupert Brooke's 4 June 1906 letter; Emil Reich 1908; Robert Lynd's 29 June 1912 review in The Nation ('said either Wilde or Mr. Max Beerbohm') as the earliest attachment to Wilde known to QI; Philip Guedalla's 12 December 1914 New Statesman piece crediting 'Quintilian or Mr. Max Beerbohm'; M. Oppenheim's 1914 ascription to Beerbohm; and Richard Ellmann's 1988 biography (quote page 106) attributing 'History never repeats itself. The historians repeat each other. There is a wide difference.' to Wilde in a footnote with no supporting citation, which other researchers have been unable to find in Wilde's oeuvre.

The full text of The Works of Max Beerbohm contains, as the opening of the essay '1880': "'History,' it has been said, 'does not repeat itself. The historians repeat one another.' Now, there are still some periods with which no historian has grappled..." The essay is signed 'London, 1894' at its foot, and '1880' appears in the book's table of contents.
The Internet Archive holds a complete downloadable scan of 'The works of Max Beerbohm', by Beerbohm, Max, Sir (1872-1956), Charles Scribner's Sons, New York, 1896.

Yellow Nineties 2.0 presents Max Beerbohm's essay '1880' as published in The Yellow Book, vol. 4, January 1895, pp. 276-283; its transcription opens 'I SUPPOSE that there is no one, however optimistic, that has not wished...' and does not contain the sentence about history not repeating itself and historians repeating one another.
Wikiquote's Oscar Wilde page contains no entry for 'History never repeats itself / The historians repeat each other' in any section, including its Attributed, Disputed and Misattributed sections.

Wikipedia states The Works of Max Beerbohm was published in 1896 by John Lane at The Bodley Head, London, and lists '1880' among its essays, which were collected from 1890s periodicals including The Yellow Book.
Wikipedia gives Max Beerbohm's dates as 24 August 1872 - 20 May 1956, describes him as an English essayist, parodist and caricaturist, and notes The Works of Max Beerbohm was published in 1896.
AllGreatQuotes publishes 'History never repeats itself. The historians repeat each other. There is a wide difference. - Oscar Wilde' with no source, work or date cited.
